doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Meeting Doc in the woods in 1965 and joining the Tonight Show band
summary: At seventeen he traded high notes with Doc and taught him Caruso exercises; later the Hamburg call, end of NBC contracts, and juggling the show with record dates and little sleep.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: I was on the Jimmy Dorsey band and we were on Long Island playing at a country club. And I was doing some Carmine Caruso exercises warming up before the gig. We had quite a few hours, maybe two or three hours before the gig started at this golf course/country club. So I went up and I’m doing some exercises, and I went up to a high F. And out of the woods a trumpet answers me with a high F. Now I’m 17 and the guys in the band are like ribbing me about oh boy Chuck, they’re a dime a dozen here in New York in the Big Apple. So then I went up to a high F sharp. Out of the woods comes a high F sharp. I’m like Jesus, now they’re getting even more on me. I go up to high G. A high G comes out. An A flat, A flat comes out. A double A, a double A comes out. Now they’re really, really ribbing me you know. And I’m thinking to myself okay enough of this nonsense, so I went up and played a double D and I held it really good, nice and strong. Dead silence out of the woods. Dead silence. And then all of a sudden you hear [scats rapidly] and I said that’s Doc, that’s got to be Doc, it has to be Doc Severinsen, not some young kid that you’re talking about in New York. So I go to the woods, and I think this other trumpet player Gene Benson went with me. And we go through the woods and that was when Doc was rehearsing his little band. So we had over an hour or so, more than that, before the gig started. So I’m sitting there with Doc and he asked me how I did that. And I told him of Carmine Caruso, I studied with Carmine, and everybody was. He was like the guru of brass instruments. Are you familiar with Carmine Caruso at all? You © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

are. Okay. So anyhow I showed him the exercises, the six notes, the harmonic series, and then the seconds, to build up you strong, that’s the muscle building exercise. And I showed that to him and I gave him that lesson in the woods. And that was, I was 17 and he was 37. He’s 20 years older than me. So then I’m on Buddy’s band — that was the first meeting. Then I’m on Buddy’s band in ’66 and I joined the band, and the Tonight Show was traveling different places. We were in Chicago and the Tonight Show was there in Chicago and Johnny and Doc, and Doc did come to the gig. Because Johnny loved Buddy. He played drums and he just loved Buddy, just loved him. So they’re sitting there and once again I meet Doc and Doc’s there and I’m playing with Shew and we’re just roaring up there with Buddy’s band. He loved it. And then of course here in L.A. I’d run into him every now and then, and then Hamburg — getting back to where I started when I got called to do the gig. So what happened is that my wife called all the other guys in the band to come to my room so it wouldn’t be a shock and I’d have my friends with me. So we went down to the bar. I was wondering why they all came to my room. It was after the gig and it’s a normal time to go schloffing, you know, go to sleep you know. So we go down to the bar and order cognac and we’re drinking cognac down there. And I go up to my room and Seely calls me and tells me that Johnny had passed away and that Doc wanted me to take Johnny’s place. So then Doc called me the next day and the rest is history, and that’s when I was on the band. Now that was a wonderful gig because there was no contract with NBC. The contracts ended when the Tonight Show moved out to L.A. In New York they were signed, you had contracts with NBC or you know they were like lifetime contracts. And that ended. And Snooky had to stay actually for a year and so did Tommy Newsom I think, a couple of guys had to stay before they moved to L.A. to finish out their contract for their buy-out. So they stayed for a year. And that’s when Jimmy Zito was on the band and they had, I don’t know who took — well they had enough trumpet players anyhow with Johnny before Snooky moved out. And then when Johnny passed Snooky was there. There was no contracts anymore with NBC or MGM or Paramount, none of them. They were all individual — you just went in and worked for the company, right? Well the gig was great because if I wanted to do records I could do records, I could send a sub to the Tonight Show. So I wasn’t being stifled as far as my doing records because I was so busy doing records. But I always made it a point to be there because I loved it so much. So I’d do the Tonight Show, but that didn’t start ‘til 1:00, 2:00 in the afternoon. So I could do a morning record date. I could work at Paramount, I mean Universal, I could work Paramount, I could do a record date and then I’d do the afternoon date with the Tonight Show and then all night I’d record and I’d work ‘til two in the morning or something like that.
When did you sleep? © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

Well that’s another thing, from two ‘til well probably four in the morning ‘til eight, three in the morning ‘til eight. I’d get four, five hours sleep. You know? And then go to work. But you know when you’re that busy doing things all the time, I was so used to it. It was no big deal. I was having so much fun you know what can I say?
